result:
At dawn, the city belongs to people who are usually invisible. A baker lifts a shutter with both hands. A nurse waits for the first bus, holding her shoes together with one frayed lace. Somewhere above them, a man opens his window and waters a plant he has almost decided to throw away.

I like this hour because nothing has yet agreed to be ordinary. Light gathers in the gutters. Pigeons inspect the pavement like severe landlords. The bread van exhales warm air, and for a moment the whole street smells faintly of toast.

We spend so much time waiting for life to become impressive. We imagine it will arrive with music, or at least with a clear set of instructions. Instead, it keeps offering us small, badly labeled parcels: a stranger’s patience, rain on a hot roof, the private comedy of missing a train by three seconds.

Perhaps attention is the closest thing we have to magic. Not the grand, concentrated kind, but the gentle decision to notice what is already here. The plant opens one new leaf. The nurse closes her eyes. The baker sets aside a misshapen loaf for himself.

By eight, the city will be loud with purpose. Everyone will seem to know where they are going. But for now, the day is still soft at the edges, and even the pigeons appear willing to reconsider. A delivery bicycle turns the corner, and its bell rings once, bright as a coin dropped into an invisible well.
